 The $25,000 Line That Taxes Social Security Has Not Moved Since 1984. A $2,170 Check Plus a $12,000 Pension Crosses It
 Maurie Backman Sat, November 7, 2026 at 1:53 AM PST 4 min read Quick Read 
 Congress set the $25,000 provisional income threshold for taxing Social Security benefits in 1984 and never indexed it, so rising benefits pull more retirees into taxation. 
 A 3.6% COLA lifts the average benefit to about $2,170 monthly, and adding a $12,000 pension pushes a single filer past the threshold. 
 The $6,000 senior deduction currently shields many retirees from benefit taxes, but it expires in 2028 unless lawmakers extend it.

 Many people look forward to claiming Social Security in retirement. But some retirees end up with a big shock when they realize that they aren't eligible to keep their Social Security checks in full. 
 Steve Heap / Shutterstock.com The reason boils down to a decades-old formula that determines whether Social Security benefits are subject to taxes or not. And as benefits increase over time, more seniors are likely to end up losing money to taxes. 
 The $25,000 threshold that's stuck in the past 
 Years ago, Social Security found itself deep in the throes of a financial crisis. Congress had to act to prevent program cuts, so reforms were implemented to allow for the taxation of benefits. 
 Since 1984, a provisional income of $25,000 for single tax filers has meant that a portion of Social Security benefits can be taxable. Provisional income is calculated as the total of adjusted gross income, tax-exempt interest income, and 50% of annual Social Security benefits. 
 The problem is that the $25,000 provisional income threshold that was established decades ago has not gotten an inflation adjustment. But benefits have. And as benefits have increased through the years, more Social Security recipients find themselves at risk of being taxed. 
 ------ 
 Can You Answer These Three Questions? 
 Americans say they need $1.46 million to retire comfortably. Whether that number fits your life depends on three questions most people never work through: 
 1. How much can you withdraw each year without running out? 
 2. When should you claim Social Security? 
 3. How much will taxes take from your 401(k) or IRA?

 Meanwhile, Social Security benefits are getting a 3.6% cost-of-living adjustment, or COLA, in 2026. That's the most generous increase to arrive in years. Once that COLA takes effect, the average monthly Social Security benefit is expected to increase to $2,170. On an annual basis, the typical Social Security recipient will get to collect $26,040. 
 Story Continues When we take half that amount, which is what's included in the formula for provisional income, we get $13,020. A $12,000 pension plus the average 2027 Social Security benefit would push a single tax-filer above the $25,000 provisional income mark, potentially subjecting a portion of their benefits to taxes. 
 Granted, if the only income to account for is a $2,170 monthly Social Security check and a $12,000 annual pension, there's not much of a tax hit to worry about. The point, rather, is that Social Security's provisional income rules are very dated, and recipients need to understand that their benefits may not be theirs to keep in full. 
 A temporary reprieve soon runs out 
 As part of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, some seniors are now eligible for a $6,000 deduction. That deduction exempts income from taxes, as all deductions do. As a result, many Social Security recipients are currently exempt from paying taxes on their monthly benefits due to having low enough provisional income. 
 But that $6,000 deduction won't last forever. Currently, it's set to expire in 2028. So if that's what's been keeping you from having your benefits taxed, you may want to gear up for a big change after 2028, especially as Social Security benefits continue to grow as COLAs come through. 
 Of course, if lawmakers vote to extend the $6,000 senior deduction, things could change. But for now, it's best to assume that taxes on Social Security might come into play – if not in 2028, then at some point in time.
